items.readable_text:
Content:
All the angles we have constructed so far have been inside the range [MATH: (-360^\circ, 360^\circ).] However, we can also construct angles outside this range.

Content:
The way we do this involves coterminal angles. Coterminal angles are different angles that appear as the same angle in the coordinate plane. For example, the angles [MATH: 0^\circ] and [MATH: 360^\circ] are coterminal because a rotation of [MATH: 360^\circ] is the same as the rotation of [MATH: 0^\circ.] In general, whenever we add or subtract a multiple of [MATH: 360^\circ,] we get a coterminal angle.

Content:
The standard way in which we draw a positive angle [MATH: \theta] in the coordinate plane is as follows:

Content:
- Subtract integer multiples of [MATH: 360^\circ] until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range [MATH: [0^\circ, 360^\circ ).]
- Draw the resulting angle in the coordinate plane.

Content:
For example, to represent the angle [MATH: 405^\circ] in the coordinate plane, we first subtract [MATH: 360^\circ\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 405^{∘} − 360^{∘} = 45^{∘}✓]

Content:
The result, [MATH: 45^\circ,] is a coterminal angle that lies in the range [MATH: [0^\circ, 360^\circ).] So, to draw the angle [MATH: 405^\circ,] we draw the coterminal angle [MATH: 45^\circ] in the coordinate plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b3095961b489cce52ef75b2b7dd84784]

Content:
Note: For every multiple of [MATH: \color{blue}360^\circ] we subtract, we make one complete rotation counter-clockwise around the origin. A rotation of [MATH: {\color{blue}360^\circ}] is the same as the rotation of [MATH: {\color{blue}0^\circ},] so it doesn't contribute to our final angle.

Content:
Here, we subtracted [MATH: {\color{blue}360^\circ}] a single time, so we make a single rotation.

sections.readable_text: The angle [MATH: \theta = \dfrac {8\pi}3] is represented in the coordinate plane in the usual way. In which quadrant does it lie?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac {8\pi}3] by subtracting integer multiples of [MATH: 2\pi] until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range [MATH: [0, 2\pi).]

[MATH: (8π)/(3) − 2π = (2π)/(3)✓]

So the angle [MATH: \dfrac {2\pi}3] is coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac {8\pi}3.] Let's draw this coterminal angle in the coordinate plane.

We see that [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3}] lies in quadrant II. Therefore, [MATH: \dfrac{8\pi}{3}] also lies in this quadrant.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find the coterminal angles of a given angle [MATH: \theta,] we add and subtract integer multiples of [MATH: 360^\circ\mathbin{.}]

Let's start by adding multiples of [MATH: 360^\circ] to [MATH: 240^\circ\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 240^{∘} + 360^{∘} = 600^{∘}✓]

There are no answer choices larger than [MATH: 600^\circ,] so we can stop here.

Now, let's subtract multiples of [MATH: 360^\circ] from [MATH: 240^\circ\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 240^{∘} − 360^{∘}|= − 120^{∘}; 240^{∘} − 2 ⋅ (360^{∘})|= − 480^{∘}✓]

There are no answer choices smaller than [MATH: -480^\circ,] so we can stop here.

So, of the given angles, the coterminal angles are [MATH: 600^\circ] and [MATH: -480^\circ.]

[MATH: (3π)/(5) + 2π = (13π)/(5)]

There are no answer choices larger than [MATH: \dfrac {13 \pi} {5},] so we can stop here.

Now, let's subtract multiples of [MATH: 2\pi] from [MATH: \dfrac {3 \pi} {5}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: (3π)/(5) − 2π|= − (7π)/(5)✓; (3π)/(5) − 2 ⋅ (2π)|= − (17π)/(5)]

There are no answer choices smaller than [MATH: -\dfrac {17 \pi} {5},] so we can stop here.

So, of the given angles, the only coterminal angle is [MATH: -\dfrac{7\pi}{5}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
All the angles we have constructed so far have been inside the range [MATH: (-360^\circ, 360^\circ).] However, we can also construct angles outside this range.

Content:
The way we do this involves coterminal angles. Coterminal angles are different angles that appear as the same angle in the coordinate plane. For example, the angles [MATH: 0^\circ] and [MATH: 360^\circ] are coterminal because a rotation of [MATH: 360^\circ] is the same as the rotation of [MATH: 0^\circ.] In general, whenever we add or subtract a multiple of [MATH: 360^\circ,] we get a coterminal angle.

Content:
The standard way in which we draw a positive angle [MATH: \theta] in the coordinate plane is as follows:

Content:
- Subtract integer multiples of [MATH: 360^\circ] until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range [MATH: [0^\circ, 360^\circ ).]
- Draw the resulting angle in the coordinate plane.

Content:
For example, to represent the angle [MATH: 405^\circ] in the coordinate plane, we first subtract [MATH: 360^\circ\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 405^{∘} − 360^{∘} = 45^{∘}✓]

Content:
The result, [MATH: 45^\circ,] is a coterminal angle that lies in the range [MATH: [0^\circ, 360^\circ).] So, to draw the angle [MATH: 405^\circ,] we draw the coterminal angle [MATH: 45^\circ] in the coordinate plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b3095961b489cce52ef75b2b7dd84784]

Content:
Note: For every multiple of [MATH: \color{blue}360^\circ] we subtract, we make one complete rotation counter-clockwise around the origin. A rotation of [MATH: {\color{blue}360^\circ}] is the same as the rotation of [MATH: {\color{blue}0^\circ},] so it doesn't contribute to our final angle.

Content:
Here, we subtracted [MATH: {\color{blue}360^\circ}] a single time, so we make a single rotation.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/71a301075b25a8497466b03b17e22a35]

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Correct Quadrant for Angles that Contain More Than One Full Rotation

Example Prompt:
The angle [MATH: \theta = \dfrac {8\pi}3] is represented in the coordinate plane in the usual way. In which quadrant does it lie?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac {8\pi}3] by subtracting integer multiples of [MATH: 2\pi] until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range [MATH: [0, 2\pi).]

[MATH: (8π)/(3) − 2π = (2π)/(3)✓]

So the angle [MATH: \dfrac {2\pi}3] is coterminal with [MATH: \dfrac {8\pi}3.] Let's draw this coterminal angle in the coordinate plane.

[IMG: /graphics/6e24a235da1b088e12f0682063d328c8]

We see that [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3}] lies in quadrant II. Therefore, [MATH: \dfrac{8\pi}{3}] also lies in this quadrant.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Constructing Negative Angles that Contain More Than One Full Rotation

Content:
The method for constructing a negative angle [MATH: \theta] outside the range [MATH: ( -360^\circ, 360^\circ )] is similar to the method for positive angles, but with one main difference: we add multiples of [MATH: 360^\circ,] instead of subtracting. So the steps are:

Content:
- Add integer multiples of [MATH: 360^\circ] until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range [MATH: [0^\circ, 360^\circ ).]
- Draw the resulting angle in the coordinate plane.

Content:
For example, we can represent the angle [MATH: -660^\circ] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: − 660^{∘} + 360^{∘}|= − 300^{∘}; − 300^{∘} + 360^{∘}|= 60^{∘}✓]

Now, we draw the angle [MATH: 60^\circ] in the coordinate plane.

Again, for every multiple of [MATH: 360^\circ] that we add, we make one complete rotation around the origin clockwise. A rotation of [MATH: {\color{blue}360^\circ}] is the same as the rotation of [MATH: {\color{blue}0^\circ},] so it doesn't contribute to our final angle.

Item 9 — Tutorial: Finding Multiple Coterminal Angles

Content:
To find a coterminal angle of a given angle [MATH: \theta,] we rotate [MATH: 360^\circ] clockwise or counter-clockwise from [MATH: \theta.] We could do this again and again, each time looping by [MATH: 360^\circ] to find an infinite number of coterminal angles:
[MATH: \theta \pm 360^\circ n,\quad \text{where } n \text{ is any integer.}]

Content:
For instance, the angles [MATH: -240^\circ,] [MATH: 120^\circ,] [MATH: 480^\circ,] and [MATH: 840^\circ] are all coterminal.

There are no answer choices smaller than [MATH: -480^\circ,] so we can stop here.

So, of the given angles, the coterminal angles are [MATH: 600^\circ] and [MATH: -480^\circ.]
